content.p: On the evening of Friday 1 June 2001, the royal family of Nepal gathered for a dinner at Narayanhiti Palace in Kathmandu. By the end of the night, King Birendra and Queen Aishwarya were dead, and seven other relatives had been killed or fatally wounded. The government inquiry that reported on 14 June named the king's own son, Crown Prince Dipendra, as the gunman. An eyewitness and some relatives said he then shot himself. Dipendra was proclaimed king while on life support, and he died on Monday 4 June, so he never answered the accusation himself. His uncle Gyanendra, who had not been at the palace, was crowned the same day.

A quarter of a century later, the case is still argued over in Nepal. Many Nepalese did not accept the official account, police officers say no postmortem reports exist, and in June 2026 the government announced that it would look at the matter again.
content.h2: The prince and the dispute over a bride
content.p: Dipendra was 29, the Eton-educated heir to a throne that his father had held for 29 years, according to The Guardian. The paper wrote that Birendra was loved by his people and worshipped as an incarnation of a god. The Guardian also reported that Dipendra collected guns as a hobby.

Accounts of what drove the family quarrel come mostly from reporting and recollection, not from a court. ABC News reported that Dipendra met Devyani Rana, a fellow student, while he was in England, and that Queen Aishwarya was determined to end the relationship and wanted him to marry a distant relative from the Shah family. The Guardian, a few days after the killings, said the queen opposed the match because Devyani's grandfather was an Indian maharajah, and described Devyani as 22 and the daughter of a leading politician. The former American deputy chief of mission Larry Dinger gave a different reason in a 2014 interview: that one of Devyani's grandmothers had been a concubine, which he said made her unacceptable to the queen. Dinger prefaced his version with "reportedly" and "the story goes", and his further claim that Dipendra offered to give up the throne is a story he relayed, not something he witnessed.
Pressure was building from another side as well. The ABC cited a newspaper article from 27 May 2001 asking why the crown prince was still unmarried and whether his place as heir was in danger.

The official inquiry, whose report the Kathmandu Post summarised in 2026, counted at least 24 royals and relatives at the dinner in Tribhuvan Sadan, a building in the palace grounds. It said Dipendra spent time alone playing billiards at about 7:30 p.m., and cited statements that he had been drinking whisky neat. By the time King Birendra entered the hall, the report said, Dipendra seemed unable to control his body, and relatives including Prince Nirajan and Prince Paras took him to his private quarters.

The Guardian drew on an account from Suraj Shamsher Rana, the late queen's brother. He was not at the killings, but he had spent days interviewing survivors in hospital. He said the prince had been "misbehaving" with a guest and that Birendra, furious, sent his son away. The inquiry added its own details of the next half hour. According to the Kathmandu Post's summary, Dipendra phoned an aide at 8:19 p.m. and asked for cigarettes. The inquiry said an attendant, Ram Krishna KC, rolled a special cigarette laced with cannabis and a second, unidentified black substance, and that it was passed in through a door of the billiards room. Telephone records showed three conversations between Dipendra and Devyani Rana, who was being treated in India at the time. She told the inquiry that his speech was slurred and she asked his aides to look in on him. The Tribune quoted the orderly, Ram Krishna KC, as saying that Dipendra vomited in the bathroom, changed into battle fatigues, and declined an offered emergency bag with the words that it was not needed.

Then, the inquiry said, he went to the billiards room armed. The Guardian, drawing on Suraj Shamsher Rana's account, listed an Uzi, an M16 rifle and a pistol, and said Dipendra fired two shots at the ceiling before turning on his father. The Kathmandu Post's summary of the report names a rifle and a 12-bore shotgun instead, so the weapons differ between sources. The report said he fired at the ceiling and a wall, shot the king, went out to the garden, came back with a rifle fitted with a light and a telescope, and fired again.

According to Suraj Shamsher Rana, Nirajan, the king's younger son, stepped in front of his brother as he went to confront their mother in the garden and said, "Don't do it, please. Kill me if you want." Nirajan was shot. Dipendra then shot the queen. The king's youngest brother Dhirendra stood in front of the gun and told Dipendra, "You have done enough damage, hand over the gun now." He was seriously wounded and, the Guardian reported, was dead by Monday. The ABC repeated both exchanges, attributing the Nirajan quotation to a witness who spoke to the New York Times.

The Guardian's list of the dead was the king, the queen, Prince Nirajan, Princess Shruti, two of the king's sisters, a brother-in-law and a cousin, with Dhirendra dying later. The inquiry report, in the Kathmandu Post's summary, named Shanti, Sharada and Jayanti Shah and Kumar Khadga Bikram Shah, the king's brother-in-law, among those killed or wounded. Others were injured, including the wife of the future king Gyanendra, who was recovering in a military hospital with a dozen armed soldiers outside, the Guardian said. Paras, Gyanendra's son, was at the dinner and was not hurt.

The commission said its account rested on statements from seven people who were there, including Princess Shobha, Paras and Dr Rajiv Shah. Captain Rajiv Raj Shahi, an army doctor and the son-in-law of Dhirendra, told reporters he watched Dipendra shoot his father and mother at close range, according to the Guardian's report of the inquiry findings.

Dinger recalled that the palace shut down all communication out of Kathmandu. The state council named Dipendra king after his father's death, The Guardian reported. Dinger said that some thought security men had killed Dipendra, but that no guard would ever admit to shooting a reigning king. The first official line was that the killings were an accident. Prime Minister Koirala spoke of an "accidental firing of an automatic weapon", and the ABC recalled that this insistence fed the rumours. The Spectator noted that a palace spokesman answered questions about how an automatic weapon nobody was holding could have killed at least eight people with the shrug "Well, these accidents happen". The state newspapers reported the king's death as a passing, and the Spectator said readers learned little more.

Dipendra died on Monday 4 June. Gyanendra was crowned within hours at the Hanumandhoka royal compound, according to the Tribune. The Guardian described a silent crowd as his procession approached the gates, and said the first reaction in Kathmandu was riots, with thousands of men shaving their heads in mourning and chanting that Dipendra was innocent. The Guardian reported that two people died and at least 19 were injured in the first day of protests, while the Tribune, citing police sources, put the death toll at four; curfews followed. The editor and two directors of the Kantipur newspaper were arrested after it printed an article by a Maoist leader critical of the new king; the ABC later said the charges were dropped after a backlash.

Gyanendra appointed a three-man panel on 4 June. The opposition leader, Madhav Kumar Nepal, resigned from it. On 6 June the king's press secretariat published its terms of reference, which allowed it to visit the scene, question those present including security staff and doctors, and examine weapons and bullets, according to the Tribune. Deviram Sharma, who headed the National Investigation Department at the time, told the Kathmandu Post that Nepal had first asked to join and then withdrew for reasons Sharma said he did not know. The Spectator saw an "evidentiary vacuum", since the bodies of most victims and the likely killer had been cremated before the work could begin, and an official told its reporter that Hindu tradition mattered more than medical science.

The two remaining members, Chief Justice Upadhyaya and Speaker Ranabhat, presented their findings at a news conference on 14 June. The Guardian said they had interviewed more than 100 people, including eyewitnesses, palace staff, weapons and forensic experts and doctors. They concluded that Dipendra had consumed alcohol and smoked cigarettes laced with drugs before killing nine people. Ranabhat said no cartridges were found at the scene other than those Dipendra used. The panel did not say in the account the Guardian received whether Dipendra shot himself, although an eyewitness and some relatives had said so.

Excerpts printed by Gorkhapatra and reported by the Tribune had one of Dipendra's aides, Raju Kumar Karki, saying the habit had worsened over the past year and a half and that the prince smoked the special cigarettes in front of everyone, including at social gatherings. Karki said he believed the supply came from within the family. The prince's other aide, Gajendra Bohara, told the panel Dipendra had been smoking such cigarettes for a year, according to the Guardian. The Tribune also reported that a Nepalese weekly, citing the military surgeon Khagendra Bahadur Shreshtha, said he had told the panel that no trace of alcohol was found in the prince's blood during surgery, a claim that sits uneasily with the report's account of heavy drinking. None of the pages consulted reconciles the two. In July 2001 the palace sacked four bodyguards of the dead king, queen and crown prince and two orderlies who worked for the prince, the Irish Times said. The report said the bodyguards knew about his habit and helped him obtain drugs.

Disbelief ran deep. Kishor Shrestha, editor of the Jana Aastha newspaper, told the Guardian that someone must have inspired or provoked the prince. Isuriman Shresta, a former chief of the royal household, told the Spectator: "It's not possible. He was not that kind of man." The Guardian noted that no evidence of other people's involvement had emerged, and that the same newspaper reported police were prevented from taking witness statements and doctors forbidden to conduct postmortems. The tourism minister, answering critics, said the panel's was the highest-level probe possible.

The Maoist leader Prachanda called the killings a "grave political conspiracy" and a "pre-planned massacre", according to the Guardian. Crowds blamed Gyanendra, who was away from the palace, and his son Paras, with the ABC describing wild rumours that they colluded to frame Dipendra. A former foreign minister claimed, the ABC said, without evidence, that India and the US had been part of a plot. In 2009, The Economic Times reported that a prisoner in Birgunj jail, serving a sentence for killing a couple, claimed to have been Dipendra's bodyguard and to have witnessed the massacre, and alleged that Gyanendra and Paras were involved. The report relayed these as claims made to a Maoist lawmaker.

Nepali Times in 2009 relayed other late accounts. Biswo Karma Shah, a maternal uncle of the queen, said an aide-de-camp who ran in raised a gun to shoot Dipendra and was pushed away by another aide, which the paper said the inquiry report did not mention and which cast doubt on the aides' testimony that they were not allowed in the room. A former high palace official told the paper it was possible someone had ordered that Dipendra be shot.
content.h2: The monarchy ends, and a case reopens
content.p: Seven years later, the Maoists emerged as the largest party in the constituent assembly, and the 240-year-old monarchy was abolished, with Gyanendra leaving the palace in June 2008, the Economic Times recounted.

In June 2026, after returning to office as home minister, Sudan Gurung announced a further investigation, saying existing reports would be reviewed first, according to HimalPress. By August, the Kathmandu Post reported, nothing had started. Ministers had not decided whether police or a new commission should lead, and officers pointed to three obstacles, namely the lack of crime-scene records, of postmortem reports and of a ballistic examination. Sher Bahadur Karki, a former police superintendent who photographed the scene, said he reached it only five days after the killings. A senior police official told the paper that the original report was the only substantial basis for a new probe, and that the key question was whether its authors had reached their conclusions freely or under pressure.
